newsitem.title: FRANCE: Carlos the Jackal in retrial for Paris shootings.
newsitem.headline: Carlos the Jackal in retrial for Paris shootings.

text.p: Notorious guerrilla "Carlos the Jackal" will face a new trial soon for the murder of two French counter-intelligence officers in Paris in 1975, justice sources said on Friday.
The sources said chief anti-terrorism investigator Jean-Louis Bruguiere has completed his additional probe into the shooting for which Carlos was handed a life sentence in his absence in 1992.
The president of the Paris appeals court is due to set a date soon for the retrial, which is statutory under French law for anyone seized after they have been convicted in their absence.

Carlos is also under investigation for a series of attacks including a 1983 railway station bombing in Marseille, which killed two people, a bombing against a high-speed train the same day in which two died, and an explosion on a Paris-Toulouse train in 1982 which killed five people.

Carlos's boldest attack was to lead the 1975 kidnapping of 11 OPEC oil ministers attending a conference in Vienna. France says he killed a total of 83 people in a series of attacks, mostly in Europe and the Middle East.
Carlos was convicted of shooting dead Raymond Dous and Jean Donatini, two officers of the DST counter-intelligence service, at a Latin Quarter flat on June 27, 1975.

He also allegedly shot dead his suspected guerrilla superior, Lebanese national Michel Moukarbal who had supplied the flat's address. Another DST officer, Jean Herranz, was badly wounded but survived.
During questioning by Bruguiere, the Venezuelan-born Carlos, whose real name is Ilich Ramirez Sanchez, denied he committed the murders, justice sources said.
Carlos has refused to answer questions about the 1975 shooting, telling Bruguiere that he could not reveal the secrets of his "revolutionary organisation".

The Paris-based Al-Watan al-Arabi magazine quoted Carlos as bragging about the killings in a 1979 interview. But since his arrest, Carlos has denied giving the interview, saying it was planted by an unspecified Arab country's secret service.
